question.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2})),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(t/2)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{csc}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}2\pi \,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[u]}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$
